sections.title: Overview
sections.contentSummary: Work completed across Milestones 6 and 7 moved the project from a collection of spreadsheet records and experimental pages into a functioning inventory application with validated transactions, permanent event history, live product information, current SDS access, and reusable browser views. Milestone 6 established the processing layer. Accepted inventory requests now update current quantities and create permanent operational events. Invalid requests remain available for diagnosis but cannot change inventory or create false event records. Milestone 7 then connected that data to a routed web application. The current interface includes Home, Inventory, Product Directory, reusable Product Detail, and SDS Directory views. The Product View combines product identity, an image, manufacturer information, inventory by location, and the current SDS record.

sections.title: Embedded Navigation Problem and Solution
sections.contentSummary: The route map worked, but page-to-page navigation became unstable when Apps Script pages were used inside an embedded environment. Problem Relative links such as ?view=inventory depended on the browser resolving the correct frame and base URL. Links could work when opened directly yet fail, disappear, or replace the wrong frame when embedded. Solution The server now provides one shared appUrl to every template. Navigation links use the complete Apps Script web-app URL and send every request back through doGet(e) and the route map. Why the problem occurred In this structure, target="_top" , target="_parent" , and relative paths can refer to different frame levels depending on how the application was opened. sections.title: Verification
sections.contentSummary: Testing covered both successful operating paths and deliberate failure cases. Received inventory increased the correct destination quantity. Used Up and Removed actions reduced the correct source quantity. Moved inventory preserved the total while changing locations. Count Corrected replaced the recorded amount with the verified count. Unknown destinations produced no partial source subtraction. Over-limit removals and moves produced no negative inventory. Rejected requests remained visible for diagnosis but created no operational event. The same Product View displayed different products when only the ID changed. Inventory-by-location displayed the correct matching records. Current SDS records and document links loaded from live sheet data. Shared navigation worked across all existing views. The existing Inventory View continued to function after routing changes.

narrative.promptingSituation: Earlier inventory versions had become patchwork, while the growing Klinswork tool set still behaved like separate experiments. Mobile scaling, cropped images, inconsistent icons, and product-image problems also limited practical use.

problemsEncountered.problem: Images became cropped after mobile scaling was corrected.
problemsEncountered.effect: Important portions of product and interface images were cut away.
problemsEncountered.resolution: Removed fixed-height cropping behavior and used height:auto with object-fit:contain.

problemsEncountered.problem: Favicon and home-screen icon behavior was inconsistent.
problemsEncountered.effect: Branding updates did not appear reliably across browsers and phones.
problemsEncountered.resolution: Separated favicon, manifest, and home-screen icon responsibilities, corrected formats and dimensions, redeployed, and accounted for caching.

problemsEncountered.problem: The Prominence product image contained a gray background and right-edge artifact.
problemsEncountered.effect: The image looked poor inside Inventory 3.0.
problemsEncountered.resolution: Recreated the edge and produced both clean and white-background versions.

sections.title: Application scope and architecture
sections.contentSummary: We began by deciding that the existing Tasker app should be replaced rather than incrementally repaired. Before writing code, we defined Work Queue 2.0's purpose, boundaries, workflow, data ownership, and relationship to the wider Klinswork tool system. Create tasks directly inside the application. Remove the old Google Form intake. Eliminate the Recommendations feature. Separate active work from completed work. Keep Work Queue compatible with other Klinswork tools. Build it as a separate project so the older Tasker deployment could remain online during development.

sections.title: Shared location architecture
sections.contentSummary: A centralized location directory was designed before the task system itself. This prevents Inventory 3.0, Work Queue, and future scheduling tools from maintaining separate copies of the same location data. Shared directory Klinswork_Locations became the common reference source for units, rooms, offices, restrooms, common areas, and other work locations. Completed coverage 8 units 163 active Work Queue locations Application-specific enablement Reusable parent-and-child relationships This was also one of the first major uses of direct spreadsheet generation and editing, substantially reducing repetitive setup work.

sections.title: Operational data structure
sections.contentSummary: A separate spreadsheet was created for Work Queue 2.0 operational data. Tasks Stores each task's current state, including ID, status, priority, category, location, description, assignee, timestamps, completion note, and archived state. Task_Activity Stores the full chronological history of task creation, starts, notes, completions, reopenings, and later changes. Settings Stores app version, default priority, completion-note requirements, notification settings, and location cache duration. Task_Templates Provides the foundation for reusable task choices that reduce typing during task creation.

sections.title: Modular Apps Script backend
sections.contentSummary: The backend was divided into focused files rather than written as one large script. Config.gs Spreadsheet IDs, sheet names, app name, version, and configuration. Code.gs Setup, diagnostics, and backend test functions. WebApp.gs Web app entry point and startup data. Validation.gs Configuration, schema, input, status, and transition validation. Utilities.gs IDs, dates, formatting, normalization, sorting, and user attribution. LocationService.gs Shared location retrieval and unit/location resolution. TaskService.gs Complete task lifecycle, spreadsheet persistence, and activity logging.

narrative.promptingSituation: The stable Work Queue release could manage tasks, but it did not yet distinguish physical inventory holders from locations, connect task completion to holder state and history, or safely support the required schema and service redesign in production.
narrative.initialUnderstanding: The project needed more than a routine feature update. It required a separate beta environment and a clearer data model linking locations, holders, products, templates, tasks, and append-only events.

sections.contentSummary: The day began with a strategic decision: stop modifying the working application directly and create a fully separate Work Queue 2.1 Beta. Assignments sheet The Assignments sheet was designed around individual dated work assignments: Assignment_ID Work_Date Employee_ID Location_ID Assignment_Type Shift_Start Shift_End Status Notes Created_At Updated_At Each assignment therefore represents: one employee on one date at one location for one shift with one status This is much more flexible than…

sections.contentSummary: We decided that the app should eventually distinguish between: the normal schedule temporary exceptions the final resolved schedule The planned resolution order is: 1. Read the employee’s regular weekly schedule 2. Read any employee-specific schedule events 3. Apply overrides for the selected date 4. Return the final resolved assignment The main schedule-event types discussed were: TIME_OFF CALL_OFF CANCEL_ASSIGNMENT REASSIGNMENT SHIFT_CHANGE EXTRA_SHIFT This allows the original assignment to remain available for history while the calendar displays the corrected result.

workCoverage.coverageDescription: Covers approximately six to seven hours of August 1, 2026 design work that transformed an implicit documentation habit into a project-aware framework. The work produced a draft document-sidecar template, a procedural summary.md template, and a twenty-step documentation workflow, while defining project records, narrative authority, project-delta reconciliation, supervisor reading paths, staged instructions, validation, publication, communication, and bootstrap limitations.

subject.mainFocus: Designing a project-aware, narrative-preserving, stateful documentation framework with separate project records, summary instructions, document sidecars, workflow specifications, supervisor reading paths, publication artifacts, and explicit authority boundaries.
subject.description: A project-aware documentation framework for preserving work narrative, project context, workflow state, structured records, publication artifacts, and supervisor-readable updates.

narrative.promptingSituation: Klinswork had accumulated substantial work across conversations, HTML updates, sidecars, screenshots, applications, repositories, catalogs, and memory, but lacked an authoritative project layer explaining what each enduring undertaking was, how it related to others, its current state, and how each new body of work changed that state.
narrative.initialUnderstanding: The immediate problem appeared to be an underspecified document-sidecar template. Review showed that the missing responsibilities could not responsibly be solved by enlarging one descriptive JSON record.
narrative.intendedOutcome: Create a coordinated documentation architecture that preserves project identity, work narrative, evidence, state changes, audience-specific views, repeatable workflow, publication materials, and durable handoffs.
narrative.approach: Distinguish document records from project records, identify summary.md as the narrative authority, constrain the sidecar to describing HTML, create a procedural summary instruction set, reconstruct the full documentation process as a twenty-step workflow, and define focused instructions at stage boundaries.

progression.title: Separated projects from documents
progression.description: Recognized that dated work updates and enduring projects require different records and authority.
progression.result: A future project-record layer became the next major structural requirement.

progression.title: Identified the authoritative narrative source
progression.description: Rejected finished HTML as the preferred future source for project understanding and selected approved summary.md instead.
progression.result: HTML, sidecar, email, image brief, and project delta can derive from one narrative source.

progression.description: Required prompting situation, changing understanding, failures, turning points, method, and supervisor callouts.
progression.result: Technical depth and supervisor skimming can coexist in one document.

progression.title: Separated descriptive and procedural artifacts
progression.description: Constrained the sidecar to document description and made the summary template an instruction set.
progression.result: Each artifact gained a clearer authority boundary.

progression.title: Formalized the entire workflow
progression.description: Encoded nine phases and twenty steps with state, inputs, outputs, validation, review, automation, and next-step rules.
progression.result: The collaboration can operate as a staged, stateful pipeline.

problemsEncountered.problem: The sidecar risked absorbing project records, workflow instructions, summary narrative, publication state, and roadmap authority.
problemsEncountered.effect: One file would become oversized in purpose and duplicate several distinct systems.
problemsEncountered.resolution: Restricted sidecar authority to describing the finished HTML and its represented project contribution.

problemsEncountered.problem: Future project context might be reconstructed from finished HTML.
problemsEncountered.effect: Downstream presentation compression could become mistaken for authoritative project understanding.
problemsEncountered.resolution: Defined project records and approved summary.md as future source context, using HTML reconstruction only for legacy bootstrap work.

problemsEncountered.problem: A list of accomplishments would flatten the method and changing understanding.
problemsEncountered.effect: Future readers could recover results but not reasoning, failed paths, or reusable lessons.
problemsEncountered.resolution: Made chronological and causal narrative mandatory in the summary and structured in the sidecar.

problemsEncountered.problem: A separate supervisor-only document could drift from the technical record.
problemsEncountered.effect: The same work would require parallel rewriting and could become inconsistent.
problemsEncountered.resolution: Embedded ordered supervisor callouts and jump navigation inside the complete HTML.

problemsEncountered.problem: Loading every project and instruction for every operation would recreate context overload.
problemsEncountered.effect: The system would become slow, confusing, and difficult to maintain.
problemsEncountered.resolution: Load durable project context plus one focused instruction set at each workflow boundary.

keyDecisions.decision: Create separate project records.
keyDecisions.reason: Project identity, purpose, scope, relationships, current state, and roadmap are durable properties.
alternativesConsidered: Infer project identity repeatedly from work updates
consequences: Formal project-record design becomes the next major milestone.

keyDecisions.decision: Preserve both Markdown and JSON.
keyDecisions.reason: Markdown supports rich narrative; JSON supports validation, indexing, automation, and targeted retrieval.
alternativesConsidered: Use one format for every purpose
consequences: Human-readable and machine-readable artifacts remain complementary.

keyDecisions.decision: Make summary.md the authoritative narrative source.
keyDecisions.reason: It is created close to the work and can preserve context before publication compression.
alternativesConsidered: Use the sidecar as the primary narrative
consequences: HTML, sidecar, email, image brief, and project delta should derive from the approved summary.

keyDecisions.decision: Retain individual sidecars and generate the catalog.
keyDecisions.reason: Individual records support correction, provenance, modular retrieval, and rebuilding.
consequences: The catalog becomes a generated aggregate rather than the only surviving copy.

keyDecisions.decision: Acknowledge missing project context during bootstrap.
keyDecisions.reason: Formal project records and roadmaps do not yet exist.
alternativesConsidered: Invent stable project IDs and roadmap items
consequences: Project identity remains provisional and uncertainty is recorded explicitly.

narrative.methodEstablished: At each workflow boundary, load the authoritative project context, the approved output from the preceding stage, and one focused instruction set; perform the transformation; validate it; record the resulting state; and hand off to the next stage.
narrative.result: Three coordinated JSON artifacts and a documented twenty-step workflow now provide the first working structure of a project-aware documentation system.
lessonsLearned: Project records and document records answer different questions.
Narrative authority should be captured before downstream publication formatting.
Descriptive schemas and procedural instruction sets should remain separate.
One complete document can support multiple reader paths.
A generated catalog should not replace its individual source records.
Explicit bootstrap uncertainty is more trustworthy than invented completeness.

sections.title: Executive Summary
sections.contentSummary: What changed This body of work addressed a persistent problem in the way Klinswork projects have been developed and documented: substantial work has been completed and described in many individual conversations, work updates, HTML pages, sidecars, screenshots, applications, repositories, and memories, but there has not yet been a stable project layer explaining what each enduring undertaking is, how it relates to the others, where it currently stands, or how a new body of work changes its state. That model was useful for describing individual HTML work-update documents, but it was not designed to represent project identity, project history, the narrative of how work unfolded, roadmap reconciliation, audience-specific relevance, reusable knowledge, or the complete documentation workflow. sections.contentSummary: The problem The existing documentation system was extensive but document-centered. Individual work updates could describe what happened during a specific period, and the cumulative catalog could make those documents searchable. sections.title: Narrative of the Work
sections.contentSummary: How the method emerged The first problem: identifying projects from documents The work began by examining an existing cumulative work-update catalog and its metadata. The catalog contained several dated updates relating to Inventory, Work Queue, Calendar, shared locations, and the documentation system itself. From that review, a distinction emerged: A work-update record describes a dated document. A project record describes an enduring undertaking. The existing catalog could show which apps and topics appeared in an update, but it could not reliably answer what the project was, what its durable goal was, how it related to other projects, what state it was in before the update, or what remained afterward. This led to the first major architectural decision: add a project layer above document records rather than trying to infer project identity repeatedly from HTML updates. sections.title: Knowledge Produced
sections.contentSummary: Reusable understanding Project-Specific Lessons A document catalog cannot substitute for project definitions. Project state must be reconciled at documentation time, not reconstructed only when work resumes. A durable summary must preserve both narrative and technical accounting. Audience-specific presentation can be layered onto one complete source document. A sidecar is most useful when its authority is clearly bounded. General Lessons Structured collaboration improves when state, context, procedure, and evidence are stored separately. Instruction sets are more useful when they describe where they operate within a larger workflow. A model does not need all information at all times; it needs the correct context at the transition between stages. Historical accuracy requires preserving failed approaches and uncertainty, not only successful outcomes.
